_note: Cambridge B2 First — Reading and Use of English, Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze), 8 gaps. One file per DENSITY, named the way every other Use of English part names them: multiple-choice-8gaps / -12gaps / -15gaps / -20gaps. Paragraphs in `text` carry NUMBERED {n} placeholders matched to the question whose `number` is n, so a renderer never counts gaps and one cannot drift onto the wrong question. Adding a text is appending an object to `tests`; adding a density is dropping in a sibling file. Each question carries `focus`, `why` and a note per distractor — Part 1 turns on collocation and fixed phrase far more often than on meaning, so a student told only WHICH answer learns the answer, not the pattern.
title: Reading and Use of English — Part 1
timing: The whole paper is 1 hour 15 minutes. Part 1 is worth 8 marks of 52.
rubric: For questions 1–8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap. There is an example at the beginning (0).

tests.title: Home and abroad
tests._text: Paragraphs carry {0} … {8} where the gaps fall. Placeholders are numbered, not positional, so a renderer never has to count them and a gap can be re-ordered without silently changing which question it belongs to.
text: After a short time living in a foreign country, I noticed conversations with locals assumed a {0} pattern. There were standard answers to the usual questions. Most questions caused little {1} — it was rather like dancing, where both partners know how to avoid {2} on each other's toes.

But, 'When are you going home?' was a question I {3} to answer, whenever I {4} my life and the direction it seemed to be {5}. In the last ten years, I had lived in a dozen countries. And I had travelled through dozens more; usually in {6} of a purpose or a person; occasionally to see the attractions.

This kind of travel is not {7} wandering, but is the extensive exploration of a wide {8} of cultures. However, it doesn't allow you to put down roots. At the back of your mind, though, is the idea of home, the place you came from.

example.why: A pattern you can foresee is a predictable one. 'Steady' describes a rate that does not change, 'main' a thing's chief part, and 'respectable' is about esteem — none of them says foreseeable.

questions.why: 'Cause trouble' is the fixed pair. The other three are things you cause far less naturally, and 'little trouble' is the idiomatic way to say something was easy.

distractors.puzzle: a puzzle is something to solve, not something a question causes
distractors.obstacle: an obstacle is placed in your way; questions do not cause them
distractors.barrier: a barrier blocks — too strong, and it collocates with 'language', not 'cause'

questions.why: 'Step on someone's toes' is the idiom, here used literally of dancing and figuratively of conversation at the same time. The idiom admits no substitute.

distractors.touching: the right general sense, but the fixed phrase is not 'touching on toes'
distractors.moving: moving on someone's toes is not English
distractors.walking: you walk on a floor, not on toes

questions.why: 'Struggle to do something' means to find it hard. Of the four, only 'struggled' takes a to-infinitive with this meaning.

distractors.worked: 'worked to answer' needs a purpose, not a difficulty
distractors.competed: you compete with someone, not to answer a question

questions.why: The gap is followed directly by an object — 'my life'. 'Consider' takes one; 'think' and 'reflect' need 'about' and 'on'. This is a preposition question wearing a vocabulary question's clothes.

distractors.believed: you believe a proposition, not a life

questions.why: A direction is something a life or a journey takes. 'Take a direction' is the pair; the others are all things done to a direction from outside.

distractors.making: you make a decision, not a direction
distractors.finding: possible in isolation, but the subject is the life itself, which takes rather than finds
distractors.seeking: seeking a direction is deliberate; the sentence describes drift

questions.why: 'In search of' is fixed. Note how close the trap is: 'in sight of' is also a real phrase, but it means near enough to see, not looking for.

distractors.sight: 'in sight of' is real English with the wrong meaning — the sharpest distractor here
distractors.inquiry: an inquiry is a formal investigation

questions.why: The sentence contrasts this travel with wandering that has no purpose, and 'aimless' is exactly purposeless. The paragraph then supplies the contrast: extensive exploration.

distractors.unreasonable: about fairness or sense, not about purpose
distractors.indefinite: about duration or vagueness, not aim

questions.why: 'A wide variety of' is the set phrase. 'Wide' fixes it — you can have a wide variety and a wide range, but not a wide difference or a wide order.

distractors.difference: 'a wide difference' is not idiomatic; differences are between two things
distractors.arrangement: an arrangement is a plan or a layout
distractors.order: 'in order of' exists, but 'a wide order of cultures' does not

tests.title: A long way home
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (6.14 4.11 3.14 5.2 5.8 4.15 7.5 7.17 1.5)
text: I had planned my return from the coast carefully. A regular bus {0} would take me to the airport in plenty of time, as long as I didn't {1} the last connection from the village. What I hadn't counted on was the exceptionally {2} traffic on the motorway that afternoon. Worse still, as a direct {3} of the storms further north, the departures board had turned into a column of red.

My flight was due to take {4} at nine. By half past eight there was still no sign of anyone being allowed on {5}, and the queue at the desk had become a crowd. Then, with only three minutes {6} before the gate was due to close, came the announcement we had all been dreading: the crew had run out of hours.

The airline found us rooms in town and handed out a leaflet urging passengers to {7} care on the icy roads. I spent the evening in a small hotel, wishing that every announcement had not ended with the words, 'We wish you a pleasant {8} home.'

example.why: A bus that runs regularly is a bus service. 'Scheme' is a plan, while 'design' and 'pattern' describe shape, not transport.

questions.why: You miss a train, bus or connection when you arrive too late for it.

distractors.avoid: means to keep away from it on purpose
distractors.fail: takes an infinitive or an exam, not a connection

questions.why: Traffic is heavy (or light) in English; this is a fixed pairing.
'As a direct result of' introduces a consequence of what follows.

distractors.conclusion: is the end of an argument or the decision you reach
distractors.reason: would need 'for' and the opposite logic
distractors.cause: the storms are the cause, so the logic is reversed

questions.why: A plane takes off when it leaves the ground.

distractors.up: 'take up' means start a hobby or fill space
distractors.round: 'take round' means to show someone a place
distractors.in: 'take in' means to understand or deceive

questions.why: 'On board' means on a plane, ship or train.
Time that is left is time remaining.

distractors.staying: is for people who do not leave
distractors.waiting: is what the passengers do, not the minutes

questions.why: 'Take care' is the fixed warning.
'A pleasant journey' is the trip itself, wished at the start of it.

distractors.route: is the line you follow, not something you enjoy
distractors.way: 'a pleasant way home' sounds like a choice of road
distractors.direction: is north, south and so on

tests.title: In charge
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (3.9 2.16 3.13 2.1 6.17 4.12 6.8 3.18 2.7)
text: When Maria joined the engineering firm, she was one of the youngest members of a {1} trained team, and she knew there was an enormous amount of {0} ahead of her. Having proved herself indispensable, she was {2} within eighteen months, and when the director fell ill it was Maria who suddenly found herself in {3} of the whole department.

Being {4} of a department, she soon discovered, is not the same as being good at your job. It is easy to {5} a mistake when everyone is waiting for your decision, and in her first month she made several. When the staff elected a {6} to complain about the new rotas, she was tempted to take it personally.

A former manager {7} her not to change anything else until she had listened to everyone. So she did. She {8} two whole weeks in one-to-one meetings with her team, and the rotas were rewritten together. She now calls it the best decision of her working life.

example.why: Work is uncountable, so it follows 'an amount of'. 'Job' is countable, and 'profession' and 'career' mean an occupation over a lifetime.

questions.why: 'Highly trained' (or skilled, qualified) is the fixed pairing.

distractors.entirely: means completely and does not grade skill

questions.why: You are promoted when you move to a higher job.

distractors.advertised: is what happens to a vacancy
distractors.announced: is for news, not a person

questions.why: 'In charge of' means responsible for.

distractors.expense: 'at the expense of' is a different phrase

questions.why: The head of a department leads it.

distractors.top: 'the top of' is a position, not a role
distractors.summit: is the top of a mountain or a meeting

questions.why: You make a mistake.

distractors.get: 'get it wrong' exists, 'get a mistake' does not

questions.why: A representative speaks for a group.

distractors.sample: is a small part used to test the whole
distractors.style: is a way of doing things

questions.why: 'Advise someone (not) to do' is the pattern.

distractors.informed: is followed by 'that' or 'of', not an infinitive
distractors.offered: means she would do something herself

questions.why: You spend time doing or in something.

distractors.involved: does not take a length of time
distractors.took: needs 'It took her two weeks to...'

tests.title: Winter in the high valley
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (3.3 5.1 4.19 5.4 8.1 8.8 4.16 7.2 3.20)
text: Walkers who come to the valley in January soon learn to read the sky. Dark clouds gathering behind the peaks usually {0} that a storm is on its way, and when they appear it is wise to turn back.

On a clear morning, though, the view is breathtaking. Snowfields {1} as far as the eye can see, and it is easy to forget that you are in a {2} and empty wilderness, hours from the nearest road. A narrow track, {3} up through the pine forest, eventually reaches the ridge.

At this time of year a thick layer of frost {4} the entire valley every morning, and the lake below the ridge freezes. Visitors should be warned, however: the ice is far too {5} to bear the weight of an adult, whatever the local children may tell you.

There is a stone hut halfway up, built to provide {6} from the harsh winter weather. If you are caught out, the golden rule is not to {7} but to make for the hut and wait. And whatever you do, start down well before the sun has {8}.

example.why: Clouds indicate, that is show, that a storm is coming. People judge, examine and rate things; clouds do not.

questions.why: Land stretches as far as the eye can see.
'A vast wilderness' is a very large one.

distractors.complete: means total, which says nothing about size

questions.why: A track or path leads somewhere.

distractors.guiding: is what a person does for you
distractors.steering: is what you do to a car
distractors.directing: is for traffic, films or people

questions.why: A layer covers a surface.

distractors.surrounds: means is all round the outside

questions.why: Ice is thin or thick.

distractors.slender: describes a person or a stem

questions.why: Shelter from the weather is protection from it.

distractors.guard: is a person or a device, not protection from weather

questions.why: 'Panic' needs no object: you panic.
The sun sets in the evening.

tests.title: Shop around
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (7.15 4.14 7.18 8.12 2.4 6.3 4.20 1.8 2.12)
text: Our local supermarket has recently begun {0} a wider range of goods, but it still pays to shop around. Prices {1} considerably from one shop to another, even for exactly the same item.

Last month I bought a winter jacket online. The price, {2} delivery, came to just over a hundred euros, which seemed a bargain. Unfortunately, it didn't {3} me: I must have put on weight over the summer. To exchange it, I was told, I would need the original {4}, which of course I had thrown away with the packaging.

The company did eventually agree to a refund, to be issued as {5} as the jacket had been inspected. That took six weeks. Is it really {6} that customers who follow the rules should wait so long for their money?

I have learnt my lesson. These days I keep a folder for receipts: a cheap thing, but remarkably {7}. And when I do shop in person, I go early, because during the sales entry is strictly {8} to fifty customers at a time.

example.why: A shop stocks the goods it sells. 'Storing' is keeping things somewhere, 'reserving' is keeping them for someone, and 'maintaining' is keeping them in good condition.

questions.why: Prices vary from one place to another.

distractors.change: means move over time, not differ between places

questions.why: 'Including' adds an item to a total.

distractors.involving: means having as a necessary part
distractors.containing: is for what is physically inside

questions.why: Clothes fit you when they are the right size.

distractors.sit: 'sit' is not used for clothes on a person

questions.why: A receipt proves you paid.
'As soon as' means immediately after.
'Is it fair that...' questions whether something is just.
Something handy is useful and convenient.
Entry limited to fifty is no more than fifty.

tests.title: The museum by the volcano
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (9.1 8.7 5.13 2.10 8.10 1.2 1.18 2.18 7.12)
text: The island is best {0} for its wines, but its small museum deserves more visitors than it gets. It houses thousands of {1}, many of them donated by local families, and some of the tools on show were made during the Bronze {2}, roughly four thousand years ago.

The most precious finds are {3} in a darkened room to protect them from the light. Among them is a bronze mirror, {4} by a farmer in 1962 while he was ploughing a field. The building itself, an old merchant's house, is {5} of the architecture that flourished on the island in the nineteenth century.

Visitors last year {6} just under twenty thousand. Few of them realise how close the museum stands to the volcano, where scientists have recently detected a sharp increase in seismic {7}. The curator is calm about it. 'We have an evacuation plan,' she says, 'and all staff are {8} to practise it twice a year.'

example.why: 'Best known for' introduces what a place is famous for. 'Thought', 'expected' and 'hoped' cannot take 'for' in this sense.

questions.why: A museum houses objects: things you can see and touch.

distractors.intentions: are what you mean to do

questions.why: The Bronze Age is the name of the period.

distractors.phase: is a stage, but not part of the name
distractors.time: is not used in the name

questions.why: Museums display objects for people to see.

distractors.revealed: means made known for the first time

questions.why: You discover something that already exists.

distractors.invented: is for things created for the first time
distractors.searched: needs 'for' and does not mean found

questions.why: 'Typical of' means a good example of a type.
'Numbered' means amounted to, as a total.

distractors.counted: is what staff do to visitors

questions.why: 'Seismic activity' is the fixed term for earthquakes and tremors.
'Be required to do' means it is compulsory.

distractors.demanded: is not used in the passive with 'to'

tests.title: First aid
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (2.3 2.11 1.15 3.5 8.4 6.5 1.14 5.7 8.13)
text: My grandmother was never very {0} about what she ate, provided it was fresh, but even she drew the line at dishes made with {1} eggs. She was just as suspicious of medicines, most of which, she insisted, were only {2} of things nobody could pronounce.

I think of her whenever I teach first aid. The first lesson is simple: a casualty who is bleeding heavily needs {3} attention, so there is no time to waste. Some trainees, it turns out, cannot cope with the mere {4} of blood, which is better discovered in a classroom than at a roadside.

Last spring I came across a minor accident myself. Two cars had been {5} in a collision at a roundabout, and luckily neither driver was more than {6} injured. One complained of a {7} neck, which can be a warning sign, so we waited for the ambulance together. She was shaken but perfectly {8} of answering every question the paramedics asked.

example.why: Someone who is particular about food is fussy about it. The other three describe work, not taste.

questions.why: Raw eggs are uncooked.
A mixture is several substances combined.
'Immediate attention' is needed at once.

distractors.first: 'first aid' is fixed, 'first attention' is not
distractors.straight: is an adverb here, not an adjective
distractors.punctual: describes people who are on time

questions.why: 'The mere sight of' means just seeing it.

distractors.vision: is the ability to see, or a dream
distractors.view: is what you see from a place

questions.why: You are involved in an accident or collision.
'Slightly injured' means not badly hurt.
A stiff neck is painful to move.
'Capable of' + -ing.

tests.title: The marathon
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (6.19 6.16 7.16 9.4 6.11 9.3 1.6 1.13 2.15)
text: After three failed attempts, our local runner has finally {0} in winning the city marathon. It {1} years of dedicated practice to reach this level, and few people know that better than her coach, a former champion himself.

I have been a {2} fan of hers since she won her first schools race, and like many others I have {3} followed her career ever since. This year the field included the current world record {4}, so few people expected her to win.

For thirty kilometres the {5} was tight. Then, on the long hill by the river, she pulled away. She was {6} the strongest runner over the final stretch, and she crossed the line almost a minute ahead. Her victory, everyone agreed, was well {7}.
Afterwards she laughed about how nervous she had been at the start. The organisers had had to {8} lots to decide who would stand in the front row, and her name was the last one out of the hat.

example.why: 'Succeed in' + -ing means manage to do it. 'Reached', 'got' and 'climbed' cannot be followed by 'in winning'.

questions.why: 'It takes (time) to...' says how long something needs.
'A big fan' is the natural phrase.

distractors.major: is formal and does not collocate with fan

questions.why: You follow something closely when you watch it carefully.
The record holder holds the record.

distractors.keeper: looks after animals or a goal

questions.why: A marathon is a race.

distractors.match: is between teams or two players

questions.why: 'By far the strongest' emphasises a superlative.

distractors.by much: is not used before a superlative

questions.why: 'Well deserved' means fully earned.
'Draw lots' means choose at random.

tests.title: The dam
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (5.15 3.2 3.16 3.8 4.4 4.9 3.7 6.1 9.5)
text: The government has still not decided {0} to build a new dam on the river or to protect the valley as a national park. Under the constitution, only Parliament has the {1} to approve a project of this size, and so far it has refused to vote.

Last year an independent panel, which {2} of six experts, was asked to study the plan. Its report was presented at an international water conference, {3} in Geneva every other year, where it attracted wide interest. Several neighbouring countries made {4} of assistance with the cost.

{5} this support, the minister responsible has delayed again and again. The decision has been {6} off so often that many villagers believe it will never be taken at all. 'We were promised a {7} announcement in the spring,' says one farmer, 'and we are still waiting.'
Whatever happens, local campaigners say, the process must be open. 'In a fair society, every citizen should be {8} before the law, from the factory owner to the shepherd.'

example.why: 'Whether to' + infinitive introduces a choice between two options. 'If' cannot be followed by 'to'.

questions.why: The power to do something is the legal right.

distractors.skill: is an ability learnt by practice

questions.why: 'Consist of' lists the members.
Conferences and meetings are held.
Offers of assistance are proposals to help.

distractors.requests: would mean they asked for help

questions.why: 'Despite' + noun shows contrast.

distractors.Since: gives a reason, not a contrast

questions.why: 'Put off' means postpone.

distractors.taken: 'taken off' is for planes or clothes

questions.why: 'A further announcement' is another one.
'Equal before the law' is the legal phrase.
